newsitem.title: GERMANY: Giant Allianz unveils frank new face.
newsitem.headline: Giant Allianz unveils frank new face.

text.p: A climate of unprecedented frankness at Allianz's shareholder meeting this week has left even the most critical of its investors baffled by the turnabout at the normally reticent insurance giant.

After years of letting information on its vast wealth trickle out slowly in terse statements, last Monday's meeting saw Allianz's chief financial officer Diethart Breipohl disclose details on group investments and assets which shareholders had all but given up demanding.
"This is not something I expected to see this century," said Leonhard Knoll, a shareholder and perennial critic of Allianz's management style.
Based in Munich, Allianz AG Holding is Europe's largest insurance group with a market value of around 60 billion marks ($39.22 billion) and an investment portfolio of dizzying proportions.

The group has about 260 billion marks invested in stocks, bonds, property and other loans. It adds to that investment at a rate of about 150 million marks a day but pays out about around 180 million marks daily in claims.
Shareholders have long sought more detail on these numbers, but Monday's disclosures marked Allianz's first ever real breakdown of its investments.
Breipohl told his audience the group's property holdings had a book value of 17.5 billion marks, of which around 10 billion concerned German properties.
The finance chief went on to concede that estimates which placed the market value of these investments at 23 to 33 billion marks were "going in the right direction."

Next on the agenda were Allianz's previously undisclosed small corporate shareholdings. Breipohl produced a list of these, which included items such as three percent of electronics and engineering giant Siemens, and said their combined market value was 3.7 billion marks.

The insurer then disclosed it held substantial stakes in several German trust companies, which in turn controlled voting rights including 36 percent in engineering group MAN and 10 percent in steelmaker Thyssen AG.
The value of these investments was more than 45 billion marks, Breipohl told an increasingly nonplussed audience.
Allianz had previously declared major shareholdings in more than 100 companies worldwide, including stakes in stock market heavyweights Deutsche Bank AG and Dresdner Bank AG.

Caught off guard by openness that many viewed as overdue, shareholders said it was clear that Allianz's plans to present its accounts according to international standards in the near future had provoked the turnaround.
International Accounting Standards do not allow German companies to hide their wealth in so-called "hidden reserves", for example, as has been common practice here.
Shareholder Knoll, who along with other shareholders has had to threaten court action in the past to force Allianz to provide information, described the unprompted revelations as a "culture shock".
Neither he, nor other shareholders, were fully happy with the level of information Allianz had provided.
"But the lights have definitely switched from red to amber," he said. ($1=1.5297 Mark)
